canonical_concept.beeja: सं (Saṃ) — the prefix itself carries the bīja energy of completeness and perfection.
canonical_concept.vyakarana: Saṃskāra is a masculine noun derived from the prefix sam- (together, completely) and the root kṛ (to do) with the suffix -a. The word carries the sense of "making perfect," "refining," and "purifying."
canonical_concept.functional_meaning: Saṃskāra operates at two levels: (1) Psychological: the mental impressions (vāsanās) left by past experiences that shape present behavior and future tendencies. These are the karmic residues stored in the causal body. (2) Sociological: the sixteen (or more) life-cycle rituals (ṣoḍaśa-saṃskāras) that mark and sanctify the major transitions of human life from conception to death.
canonical_concept.dhatu: सम् + कृ (Sam + Kṛ) — Sam (together, completely, perfectly) + Kṛ (to do, to make). That which is perfectly made; that which refines and purifies.
canonical_concept.nirukta: "Saṃskriyate anena iti saṃskāraḥ" — that by which one is refined/purified. Saṃskāra has three meanings: (1) mental impression (psychological), (2) life-cycle ritual (sociological), (3) refinement/purification (philosophical).
canonical_concept.tattva: Saṃskāra-Tattva — the principle of refinement, impression, and ritual transformation. Saṃskāras operate at two levels: the psychological (mental impressions that shape character) and the sociological (life-cycle rituals that mark transitions).

claims.value: In Yoga philosophy: saṃskāras are the residual impressions in the citta (mind-stuff) that create habitual patterns of thought and behavior. They are the mechanism through which karma operates across lifetimes. In Vaiśeṣika: saṃskāra is one of the twenty-four qualities (guṇas) — the quality of elasticity or residual impression. In Mīmāṃsā: saṃskāra is the purificatory ritual that makes a person fit for Vedic study and ritual.

provenance.source_text: Gṛhyasūtras (Āśvalāyana, Pāraskara — primary texts on saṃskāra rituals)

claims.value: In Purāṇic cosmology: saṃskāras are the impressions accumulated across multiple lifetimes that determine the soul's next birth. The concept of janma-saṃskāra (birth impressions) — the soul carries its saṃskāras from life to life.

provenance.source_text: Gṛhyasūtras (Āśvalāyana, Pāraskara — primary texts on saṃskāra rituals)

claims.value: In Yoga psychology: saṃskāras are the seeds of future mental activity. They create vāsanās (latent tendencies) that drive behavior. The goal of yoga is to burn all saṃskāras through the fire of knowledge (jñāna-agni) and meditation. The concept of saṃskāra-śuddhi (purification of impressions) is the psychological goal of spiritual practice.

provenance.source_text: Gṛhyasūtras (Āśvalāyana, Pāraskara — primary texts on saṃskāra rituals)

claims.value: The concept of saṃskāra in governance: the ruler's saṃskāras (character formed by upbringing and education) determine the quality of governance. The Arthaśāstra prescribes specific saṃskāras (educational rituals) for the prince. The concept of rāja-saṃskāra (royal consecration) — the coronation ritual that transforms a person into a king.

provenance.source_text: Gṛhyasūtras (Āśvalāyana, Pāraskara — primary texts on saṃskāra rituals)

claims.value: In Āyurveda: saṃskāras (mental impressions) are a cause of mental disease. The concept of saṃskāra-cikitsā (treatment through ritual purification). The prenatal saṃskāras (garbhādhāna, puṃsavana, sīmantonnayana) are considered important for the child's health.

provenance.source_text: Gṛhyasūtras (Āśvalāyana, Pāraskara — primary texts on saṃskāra rituals)

claims.value: The concept of saṃskāra in mathematics: the refinement of mathematical knowledge through successive approximations. The concept of saṃskṛta (refined) language — Sanskrit itself is the "refined" (saṃskṛta) language, as opposed to Prakrit (natural/unrefined).

provenance.source_text: Gṛhyasūtras (Āśvalāyana, Pāraskara — primary texts on saṃskāra rituals)

claims.value: In Jyotiṣa: the birth chart (janma-kuṇḍali) reflects the saṃskāras brought from past lives. The concept of saṃskāra-yoga (combinations indicating strong past-life impressions) in Jyotiṣa.

provenance.source_text: Gṛhyasūtras (Āśvalāyana, Pāraskara — primary texts on saṃskāra rituals)

claims.value: In metallurgy: saṃskāra is the process of refining metals — removing impurities to reveal the pure metal. The concept of dhātu-saṃskāra (metal refinement) mirrors the spiritual concept of self-refinement.

provenance.source_text: Gṛhyasūtras (Āśvalāyana, Pāraskara — primary texts on saṃskāra rituals)

claims.value: The sixteen saṃskāras (ṣoḍaśa-saṃskāras): Garbhādhāna (conception), Puṃsavana (fetal rite), Sīmantonnayana (hair-parting), Jātakarma (birth), Nāmakaraṇa (naming), Niṣkramaṇa (first outing), Annaprāśana (first solid food), Cūḍākaraṇa (first haircut), Karṇavedha (ear-piercing), Vidyārambha (beginning of education), Upanayana (sacred thread), Vedarambha (beginning of Vedic study), Keśānta (first shaving), Samāvartana (graduation), Vivāha (marriage), Antyeṣṭi (funeral rites).

provenance.source_text: Gṛhyasūtras (Āśvalāyana, Pāraskara — primary texts on saṃskāra rituals)

claims.value: The potter's wheel symbolizes saṃskāra — the clay (raw human being) is shaped by the potter's hands (saṃskāras). The fire symbolizes saṃskāra's purifying function. The seed symbolizes saṃskāra's potential — impressions are seeds that will bear fruit.
